title: Three dialects, one sentence
spec: M01 · the tool-use loop, run three times
intro: Same question, same tool file, three SDKs. Watch where the wire formats diverge — and where they land on a character-for-character identical answer.

provenance.source: a narrated run of the three agent files shipped in M01 Step 2; the code, commands and final replies are the module's own, the per-round-trip log lines are reconstructed (the module's checkpoint tells you to add them)

foot: Run it for real: copy the six tabs from Step 2 — Declare the Tool & Run the Loop, drop acme_tools.py beside them, and run all three.

steps.title: One tool, three declarations
narrative: Everything up to the SDK import is shared. All three scripts import the same acme_tools.py, send the same system prompt, and ask the same sentence: "Hi, where is my order AC-1042?" The Python function they call is byte-identical across the three files.

The divergence starts at the moment you describe that function to the model. Anthropic wants a key called input_schema. Gemini wants the same JSON Schema wrapped in a FunctionDeclaration inside a Tool. OpenAI wants it flat, with additionalProperties: false bolted on.
Toggle Before / After. Before is everything the three files agree on; after is the only block that actually moves.
steps.youDo: Open the three agent_*.py tabs side by side and read only the TOOLS / order_tool block in each.

state.label: what moves between the three files

data.system: You are Acme Support. Use tools to answer order questions accurately.
data.user message: Hi, where is my order AC-1042?
data.loop shape: call -> tool requested? -> run it -> feed result back -> repeat

views.text: The tool returns {"error": "..."} rather than raising — a deliberate choice you will see pay off in step 4.

data.name: get_order_status
data.description: Look up the current status of an order by its order ID (e.g. AC-1042).

views.text: The schema body never changes — only the key it is filed under. That is the whole of the incompatibility: four field names, not four mental models.

steps.title: "Did it call a tool?" — three truth tests
narrative: Round-trip one comes back. Now each script has to answer the same question — did the model ask for a tool, or is this the final answer? — and each SDK makes you ask it differently.

Anthropic puts it on the response envelope: stop_reason == "tool_use". Gemini hands you a convenience list, resp.function_calls, and you check whether it is empty. OpenAI makes you filter the output array for items of type function_call.

The arguments arrive differently too, and this is the one that bites: Anthropic and Gemini give you a parsed dict (block.input, fc.args), while OpenAI gives you a JSON string you have to json.loads yourself.
steps.youDo: Add one line inside each loop — print(resp.stop_reason) / print(resp.function_calls) / print([i.type for i in resp.output]) — then run all three.
steps.claudeSays: All three models reach the same decision on the same sentence: they cannot answer without the tool, so they emit a request naming get_order_status with order_id="AC-1042".

before.title: THREE TESTS — same decision, three spellings

steps.title: Hand the result back — and they converge
narrative: You run the function. It returns the same dict in all three scripts, because it is the same function: {"order_id": "AC-1042", "status": "shipped", "carrier": "UPS", "eta": "Tuesday"}.

Now the return leg, which is where beginners lose an afternoon. Anthropic threads the result back through a role: "user" message as tool_result blocks — yes, a user turn. Gemini uses a dedicated role: "tool" Content carrying functionResponse parts. OpenAI appends standalone function_call_output items, keyed by call_id and not id.

Round-trip two returns text. Look at the bottom of the terminal: three different wire formats, three different SDKs, one sentence. That is the entire thesis of this course, and it is two round-trips deep.

views.text: Two round-trips is the checkpoint. If a script answers in one and quotes a tracking number, it never called the tool — it invented the answer, and your tool description is too vague to force the lookup.

steps.title: AC-9999 — the failure that isn't a crash
narrative: Change the question to "Where is order AC-9999?" and the fixture has no such order. Because get_order_status returns {"error": "..."} instead of raising, nothing in your loop breaks — the model simply reads a bad result and apologises.

Here the three SDKs diverge one last time, and only cosmetically. Anthropic gives you a dedicated flag, "is_error": True on the tool_result block, so the model knows this is a failure and not data. Gemini and OpenAI have no such flag: the error text rides in the ordinary result field and the model works it out from the words.

The flag changes the wire format, not the outcome. All three recover, and all three say the same thing. What would not survive is a raise — that crashes in your loop, before the model ever gets a chance to be helpful.
steps.youDo: Change the last line to run_agent("Where is order AC-9999?") and run all three again.
steps.claudeSays: Reads the error dict as the tool's answer, does not retry the lookup, and asks the customer to check the order number instead.

terminal.text: python agent_anthropic.py   # "Where is order AC-9999?"

get_order_status(order_id="AC-9999")
  -> {"error": "No order found with id AC-9999."}
anthropic  tool_result  is_error=True   content={"error": "No order found with id AC-9999."}
gemini     functionResponse  response={"result": {"error": "No order found with id AC-9999."}}
openai     function_call_output  output='{"error": "No order found with id AC-9999."}'

I couldn't find an order with ID AC-9999. Could you double-check the number?
Acme order IDs look like "AC-1042" — you'll find it in your confirmation email.
same recovery from all three · loop never raised · 2 round-trips each

before.title: WHERE FAILURE CAN HAPPEN — and who handles it

cells: the loop dies before the model sees anything

view.text: The three dialects differ in exactly four places — the schema key, the "did it call a tool?" test, the argument type, and the role the result rides back in. Everything above and below that is yours and portable. The honest caveat: this walkthrough ran the loop as while True, and a model that keeps requesting tools will spin it forever at one paid API call per turn. Ship for _ in range(8) with a "let me get a human" fallback instead — that is what M03's loop already does.
